title: How it works
text: The extension is five files in three places, and each runs at a different time.

title: How it works
text:
At render time
You turn the extension on by listing issue-comments under filters: and giving it an issue-comments: block in _quarto.yml or a page’s front matter. For each page, the Lua filter:

stops unless the output is HTML and the block has an endpoint;
works out the remaining settings, falling back to the document’s first author for owner;
attaches issue-comments.js and issue-comments.css to the page; and
writes the settings into the page’s <head> as window.ISSUE_COMMENTS.

Nothing is sent anywhere at render time. A page without the block, or a PDF or Word render, is left exactly as it was.

title: How it works
text:
In the reader’s browser





sequenceDiagram
  actor R as Reader
  participant P as Page (issue-comments.js)
  participant S as Apps Script relay
  participant G as GitHub API
  R->>P: highlights text
  P-->>R: shows 💬 Comment beside the selection
  R->>P: clicks it, types name and comment
  P-->>R: shows the exact issue (preview)
  R->>P: Post publicly
  P->>S: POST JSON as text/plain
  S->>S: honeypot, passcode, site, length and hourly checks
  S->>G: POST /repos/owner/repo/issues (your token)
  G-->>S: 201 Created, issue number and URL
  S-->>P: { ok: true, number, url }
  P-->>R: Thanks! Posted as issue 12






The script watches the selection. When it covers at least two characters inside the page’s main content, it records the text (cut to 1,500 characters), the nearest heading and that section’s id, and places the button under the end of the selection. The dialog has three stages: edit, preview (unless preview: false) and done. The reader’s name is saved in their own browser so they don’t retype it.
The request is sent as text/plain so the browser does not first send a CORS “preflight” request, which Apps Script cannot answer.

title: How it works
text:
On the relay
doPost reads your Script Properties, runs its checks, builds the issue text, and creates the issue with your token. It always answers with JSON of the form { ok, error } or { ok, number, url }, which the page shows to the reader. doGet exists only so that opening the /exec URL in a browser confirms the deployment is live.

title: How it works
section: Two copies of the issue format
text:
Two copies of the issue format
The preview has to show exactly what will be posted, but the issue is built on the relay. So the format is written twice: buildIssue_ in Code.gs, and issueTitle and fillPreview in issue-comments.js. A change to one needs the same change to the other. The relay page lists where the two currently differ.

title: 5. Apps Script relay
text: The relay is a Google Apps Script web app that you deploy from your own Google account. It receives each comment, checks it, and creates the GitHub issue with your token. It is the only part that holds a secret, so it is the part to read most carefully.

title: 5. Apps Script relay
text:
Settings
All configuration lives in Script Properties, which only you can see. Changing a property takes effect on the next request, with no redeployment.

apps-script/Code.gs, lines 2–13
* issue-comments relay: receives a reader's comment from the Quarto page and
* files it as a GitHub issue using YOUR token. The token stays here, in
* Script Properties, and is never sent to the browser.
*
* Script Properties (Project Settings > Script Properties):
*   GITHUB_TOKEN   fine-grained token, this repo only, Issues: Read and write
*   GITHUB_REPO    owner/repo
*   SITE_PREFIX    optional, e.g. https://owner.github.io/repo/  (rejects other pages)
*   PASSCODE       optional, only if you set `passcode: true` in Quarto
*   LABEL          optional, defaults to "reader-comment"
*   MAX_PER_HOUR   optional, defaults to 20 (all readers combined)
*/

text:
Updating the deployment
After changing Code.gs, use Deploy → Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version. That keeps the same /exec URL. New deployment gives a new URL, which every site using the relay would then need.

title: 1. Manifest
text: The manifest tells Quarto that _extensions/issue-comments/ is an extension and that what it contributes is one filter.

title: 1. Manifest
text:
What each field does

title, author and version are shown by quarto add and quarto list extensions. The version here should match the one the filter gives its HTML dependency (see the Lua filter), so the browser does not keep a cached copy of an older script.
quarto-required: ">=1.4.0" makes Quarto refuse to run the extension on an older version rather than fail partway through. The filter relies on Quarto’s Lua API (quarto.doc.add_html_dependency, quarto.doc.include_text, quarto.json.encode and quarto.log.warning), so this floor should be raised if the filter starts using anything newer.
contributes: filters lists one Lua filter. A site turns it on by naming the extension, issue-comments, under filters:; Quarto then finds this manifest and runs issue-comments.lua.

Nothing else is declared. The JavaScript and CSS are not listed here because the filter attaches them itself, and only to HTML pages that have commenting configured.

title: 1. Manifest
text:
What quarto add installs
quarto add VagishHemmige/quarto-commenting-extension copies every folder under the repository’s _extensions/, so this folder must stay the only one there. That is why this website’s own tools live in site-tools/ rather than _extensions/.

title: 4. Styles
text: The stylesheet gives the buttons and dialog a look that fits the site. Every class starts with ic-, so it cannot clash with the site’s own styles.

title: 4. Styles
text:
Following the site’s theme
Colours come from the Bootstrap variables that Quarto’s HTML themes define (--bs-body-bg, --bs-primary and so on), each with a fallback. So the buttons and dialog take on the site’s theme, including a dark theme, and still look reasonable on a page without Bootstrap.

issue-comments
text:
issue-comments is a Quarto extension. A reader highlights a passage on your site, types their name and a comment, checks a preview, and clicks Post publicly. The comment becomes an issue in a GitHub repository you choose, with the passage quoted and a link back to its section. Readers need no GitHub account, or any account.
flowchart LR
  A["Reader's browser<br/>(issue-comments.js)"] -- "name, comment,<br/>passage, page" --> B["Google Apps Script<br/>relay (Code.gs)<br/>holds your token"]
  B -- "GitHub REST API" --> C["Issue in<br/>your repository"]
Your GitHub token stays in an Apps Script project that you own and is never sent to the page.

title: issue-comments
text:
Using it
Installation and the ten-minute setup are in the README. In short:
quarto add VagishHemmige/quarto-commenting-extension
then deploy apps-script/Code.gs as a web app and add its URL to _quarto.yml.

title: issue-comments
text:
What this site is for
This site explains how the extension works, file by file, for anyone who wants to check it before trusting it with their token, change it, or contribute. The code on every page is read from the repository’s files when the site is built, so what you see is the code that quarto add installs.

How it works follows one comment from a highlighted passage to a GitHub issue.
Security and privacy sets out what each guard protects against, and what it does not.
The Source code pages take each of the five files in turn, in the order a comment passes through them.

title: issue-comments
text:
Status
Version 0.2.0. It has been used end to end on a live GitHub Pages site, with comments arriving as issues. It has no automated tests.

title: 3. Browser script
text: The script runs in the reader’s browser. It shows the 💬 Comment button next to a selection, runs the comment dialog, and sends the comment to the relay. It has no dependencies, and the whole file is wrapped in a function so that nothing except what the filter set (window.ISSUE_COMMENTS) is shared with the page.

title: About
text:
Contributing
Report a problem or suggest a change by opening an issue. Changes reach main through pull requests.
A change to the issue format has to be made in two places, buildIssue_ in apps-script/Code.gs and issueTitle and fillPreview in issue-comments.js; see How it works.

title: About
text:
How this site is built
The site is a Quarto website in the same repository as the extension. _quarto.yml and index.qmd are at the root, the other pages are in quarto/, and the rendered site is committed in docs/ and served by GitHub Pages. quarto add copies only _extensions/issue-comments/, so none of the site reaches people who install the extension.
The code on each page is not pasted in. Each block names a file and a line of text it starts at, and a small filter, site-tools/source-snippet.lua, reads those lines from the file when the site is rendered and links them to the same lines on GitHub. If a file is renamed or the starting line changes, the render fails with a message naming the page and file, so the site cannot silently fall out of date. The prose still has to be updated by hand when the code’s behaviour changes, in the same pull request.
To rebuild it, run quarto render in the repository’s root and commit docs/.

title: Security and privacy
text: The extension lets anyone on the internet cause your GitHub account to open an issue. This page sets out what limits that, so you can judge whether the limits are enough for your site.

title: Security and privacy
text:
The token
The GitHub token is stored only in the Apps Script project’s Script Properties. The page never receives it: the filter writes only endpoint, owner, contact and three on/off settings into the page, and the relay’s replies contain only ok, error, number and url.
The relay is deployed to Execute as: Me, so it acts as you, and Who has access: Anyone, so readers can reach it without signing in. Anyone who finds the /exec URL in your page source can therefore send it requests. What protects you is the token’s scope. A fine-grained token limited to one repository with Issues: Read and write and nothing else means that, even if the relay had a bug or the token leaked, the damage is limited to issues in that one repository.

title: Security and privacy
text:
Guards on the relay








Guard
Stops
Does not stop




Hidden “website” field (honeypot)
simple bots that fill in every field; they get a fake success
anyone who reads the page’s code


SITE_PREFIX
other sites embedding your relay; casual reuse of the URL
a request crafted by hand, since the page address is supplied by the sender


PASSCODE (optional)
strangers, if you share the passcode only with intended readers
anyone you’ve told it to


MAX_PER_HOUR (default 20)
a flood of issues
a slow trickle; one person using up the allowance for everyone


Length limits (name 80, comment 5,000, passage about 1,600, page 500 characters)
oversized issues
—


@ mentions neutralised
comments pinging GitHub users from your account
—



The hourly limit counts all readers together, in clock hours, and the count lives in Apps Script’s cache, which Google may clear early. Treat it as a brake, not a guarantee. If spam does arrive, turn on the passcode, lower MAX_PER_HOUR, or close the deployment.

title: Security and privacy
text:
Guards on the page

Everything a reader types, and every setting, is put on the page as text (textContent), never as HTML, so a comment or a setting cannot inject markup.
The contact link is used only if it is an http, https, mailto or relative address, so a javascript: URL in the settings cannot run.
The filter escapes </ in the settings it writes into the page, so a value cannot close the <script> tag early.

title: Security and privacy
text:
What readers’ data goes where
A reader’s name, comment, the highlighted passage, the section heading and anchor, and the page address go to the relay, and from there into a public issue (all except the anchor and page, which form the section link). Their name is also kept in their own browser’s localStorage to save retyping. Nothing else is collected: no email, no GitHub identity, no cookies. Apps Script does not give the script the reader’s IP address, though Google keeps its own request logs.
Readers are told before posting that the comment is public, that you post it, and that they cannot edit or delete it themselves; they are shown the exact issue first unless you set preview: false.

title: Security and privacy
section: Limits that follow from the design
text:
Limits that follow from the design

Names are not verified. Anyone can type any name.
Comments are posted as typed. GitHub renders Markdown in the comment and passage, so a reader can add links or formatting. The name and section heading are escaped.
Readers are not notified of replies, because they have no GitHub identity in the issue.

title: 2. Lua filter
text: The filter runs once for each page Quarto renders. It decides whether the page gets commenting, settles the settings, and adds the script, the styles and the settings to the page. It does not change the page’s content.

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
The settings it accepts
The comment at the top of the file is the reference for the issue-comments: block. Only endpoint is required.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 1–10
-- issue-comments: let readers highlight text and send a comment that is
-- filed as a GitHub issue by a Google Apps Script relay.
--
-- issue-comments:
--   endpoint: https://script.google.com/macros/s/XXXX/exec   # required
--   owner: Jane Doe              # who posts the issues; defaults to `author`
--   contact: https://...         # how readers reach you (URL or mailto:)
--   preview: true                # show the exact issue before posting
--   passcode: false              # ask readers for a shared passcode
--   page-button: false           # also show "Comment on this page"

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Reading YAML values
Quarto hands settings to a filter as Pandoc values, not plain strings: owner: Jane Doe arrives as a list of words. str turns any value into text, and treats an empty value as missing so that contact: "" behaves like no contact at all.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 12–17
local function str(v)
  if v == nil then return nil end
  local s = pandoc.utils.stringify(v)
  if s == "" then return nil end
  return s
end

bool gives each on/off setting its default when it is absent. YAML true arrives as a Lua boolean, but a value written as a string ("yes", "true") is accepted too.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 19–24
local function bool(v, default)
  if v == nil then return default end
  if type(v) == "boolean" then return v end
  local s = pandoc.utils.stringify(v)
  return s == "true" or s == "yes"
end

first_author provides the default owner. In Quarto, author can be written as a single name, a list of names, or a list of maps with a name field (the form most templates use); this takes the first name in any of the three.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 27–32
local function first_author(meta)
  local a = meta["author"]
  if type(a) == "table" and a[1] ~= nil then a = a[1] end
  if type(a) == "table" and a["name"] ~= nil then a = a["name"] end
  return str(a)
end

title: 2. Lua filter
section: Deciding whether the page gets commenting
text:
Deciding whether the page gets commenting
The work happens in Meta, which Pandoc calls once with the page’s metadata. It returns early, leaving the page unchanged, for any non-HTML output, so PDF and Word renders of the same source are untouched.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 35–37
if not quarto.doc.is_format("html") then
  return meta
end

A page with no issue-comments: block, or with issue-comments: false, is also left alone. That is how a page can opt out of a site-wide setting. A block that is not a map (for example issue-comments: true) is a mistake, so it produces a warning rather than silently doing nothing.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 39–46
local cfg = meta["issue-comments"]
if cfg == nil or cfg == false then
  return meta
end
if type(cfg) ~= "table" then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: expected a map with at least `endpoint`.")
  return meta
end

Without an endpoint there is nowhere to send comments, so the page is left alone with a warning.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 48–52
local endpoint = str(cfg["endpoint"])
if endpoint == nil then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: no `endpoint` set; commenting is disabled.")
  return meta
end

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Settling the settings
These are the six values the browser script receives. The keys are camel case (pageButton) because they become JavaScript properties. A missing contact is allowed, since readers are still told who to contact, but Quarto warns because they would have no link to follow.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 54–64
local settings = {
  endpoint = endpoint,
  owner = str(cfg["owner"]) or first_author(meta),
  contact = str(cfg["contact"]),
  preview = bool(cfg["preview"], true),
  passcode = bool(cfg["passcode"], false),
  pageButton = bool(cfg["page-button"], false),
}
if settings.contact == nil then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: no `contact` set; readers won't see how to reach you.")
end

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Loading the script and styles
add_html_dependency copies the JavaScript and CSS into the site’s site_libs/ folder and links them from the page. The version is part of the folder name there, so it should be kept in step with the manifest.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 66–71
quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({
  name = "issue-comments",
  version = "0.2.0",
  scripts = { "issue-comments.js" },
  stylesheets = { "issue-comments.css" },
})

title: 2. Lua filter
section: Passing the settings to the page
text:
Passing the settings to the page
The settings go into the page’s <head> as a global variable that the script reads when it starts. Encoding them with quarto.json.encode handles quotes and special characters. The extra replacement of </ covers the one case JSON does not: a value such as contact: "</script><script>…" would otherwise end the script tag and let the rest run as HTML.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 73–76
-- Escape "</" so values cannot close the script tag.
local json = quarto.json.encode(settings):gsub("</", "<\\/")
quarto.doc.include_text("in-header",
  "<script>window.ISSUE_COMMENTS = " .. json .. ";</script>")
